title: Only with a teacher
hook: both Mahamudra and Dzogchen are traditionally learned face to face

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dzogchen, and your line, already complete. Did a mirror remind you of anything? Two days, two great teachings, and today, how both are passed on. Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

Two people stop on a woodland path. One of them whispers: there's an owl. The other looks. Bark, branches, leaves, more bark. Nothing. The first one steps behind, lines up a finger beside the other's cheek, and points. Third branch up. Where it forks. That gray lump. And all at once the lump has eyes, and a face, and it can't be unseen. A field guide could have described that owl for a year. It took a person, a finger, and a moment, side by side. Tibetan teachers say the deepest teachings pass the same way. Today: only with a teacher.
screen: `THERE'S AN OWL.` → `FOLLOW MY FINGER.` → `NOW IT CAN'T BE UNSEEN.`

segments.voice: First, the pointing out. Both Mahamudra and Dzogchen speak of a moment when a teacher points out the nature of the student's own mind. The first of Garab Dorje's statements, from yesterday, was: be introduced directly to your own nature. An introduction needs someone to make it. Tibetan teachers explain why: the mind's nature is so close and so simple that we look straight past it, the way an eye can't see itself. Second, a story the Kagyu tell. Naropa was a great scholar, tradition says, honored for his learning. Then he met the wild teacher Tilopa, and for years Tilopa put him through hardship after hardship, and taught him almost nothing in words. In the story, the moment finally came when Tilopa struck him with a sandal, and Naropa saw. What a lifetime of reading had circled around, one face-to-face moment opened. Third, the care on both sides. The guru yoga lesson met the advice to examine a teacher. Here it runs both ways: Tibetan texts on teacher and student advise each to examine the other before the relationship begins. A pointing out only means something from a teacher whose own life shows the teaching. Fourth, what's left for everyone else. Books, recordings, and lessons like this one can describe these teachings and prepare the ground. Teachers in both lineages say the rest happens in person. Like the owl on the third branch, some things need a finger beside your cheek, not another page. Saying so plainly is part of honoring the teaching.
screen: `A TEACHER POINTS OUT THE MIND.` · `NAROPA, TILOPA AND THE SANDAL.` · `EXAMINE EACH OTHER FIRST.` · `SOME THINGS PASS ONLY IN PERSON.` · then, large: `FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor what you can't learn alone. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Then bring to mind one thing you only learned because someone showed you, side by side. Tying a shoe. Riding a bike. A prayer. A recipe. How to be kind to someone who's grieving. See their hands, their face, the moment it clicked. Let some thanks go toward them, wherever they are now. The bell holds the time.
Only with a teacher. In Tibetan tradition, Mahamudra and Dzogchen are learned face to face, when a trusted teacher points out the nature of the student's mind. Today's word.
Your line: face to face. Today, show one person something in person instead of sending a link: how to fix it, where to find it, how you do it. Day one thousand three hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, Mahamudra and Dzogchen are traditionally received from a qualified teacher, often after preliminary practices, in a pointing-out instruction given in person; teacher and student are advised to examine each other before the relationship begins.

notes: Naropa story: the sandal blow and 'years' of hardship are told as tradition; confirm the details (versions differ).
Advice that teacher and student examine each other, possibly for a long time: attributed generally to Tibetan texts (e.g. Fifty Verses on the Guru); confirm.
The eye-can't-see-itself image is given as how Tibetan teachers explain it; confirm.
The script says the traditions themselves hold that books can only prepare the ground; confirm this is fair to both Kagyu and Nyingma.
The owl-on-a-branch image is the writer's illustration, not a traditional one.
